H1.text: A stone whirls on a string. The Moon circles the Earth. A car takes a bend.

H2.text: All three go round. So what keeps pulling each one in?

H3.text: Aarav takes the turn at the college gate on his bicycle. Slowly, it is easy.

H4.text: Faster, and his tyres slide out. What holds him on the curve, and why does it let go?

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will find his top speed with one short formula.

P1.text: So what is a centripetal force?

P2.text: In episode forty eight, going round needed an acceleration toward the centre, v squared over r.

P3.text: By Newton's second law, an acceleration needs a net force the same way.

P4.text: That net force toward the centre is the centripetal force.

P5.text: It is not a new kind of force. It is a job that some real force must do.

P6.text: A string's tension. The road's friction. Gravity. Or the push of a wall.

S1.text: A half kilogram stone on a one metre string goes round a smooth table, seen from above.

S2.text: At two metres per second, the string pulls with two newtons, toward the centre.

S3.text: Now speed up to four metres per second. Watch the orange arrow.

S4.text: The tension jumps to eight newtons. Double the speed, four times the pull.

S5.text: On the graph, the dot climbs a curve. The tension grows with v squared.

S6.text: Slow-mo replay. Now we cut the string.

S7.text: The pull is gone. The stone does not fly outward. It carries straight on, along the tangent.

S8.text: The string alone was bending its path. That inward pull was the centripetal force.

D1.text: Now let's write it down, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. At speed v on a circle of radius r, the acceleration is v squared over r, toward the centre.

D3.text: Step two. Newton's second law. The net force equals mass times acceleration.

D4.text: Step three. So the net inward force, F c, is m v squared over r. With v equal to omega r, it is m omega squared r.

D5.text: Step four. Units. Kilograms times metres per second squared, which is newtons.

T1.text: Remember this. Centripetal force is not a new force. It is the net inward pull of real forces.

C2.text: On a string, tension pulls the stone in. Spin faster and it just pulls harder, until it snaps.

C3.text: On a flat road, only friction pushes the car in, and friction has a limit, mu m g. So m v squared over r can be at most mu m g.

C4.text: Cancel m. The top speed is root mu r g, and the mass has gone.

C5.text: Now you try. A heavy truck takes the same flat curve as a small car. Is its top safe speed lower, or the same? Pause and decide.

C6.text: The same! The truck needs more friction, but it presses harder on the road, so it gets more.

M1.text: One more. The Moon goes round the Earth. What supplies its centripetal force? Pause and think.

M2.text: Gravity! The Earth's pull does the whole job. No extra force is needed.

R1.text: So why do Aarav's tyres slide out? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. To go round, the car needs an inward force of m v squared over r.

R3.text: Two. On a flat road, only friction can give it, and at most mu m g.

R4.text: Three. As the car speeds up, the force it needs grows with v squared.

R5.text: Four. Past the limit, friction cannot bend the path enough. The car runs wide, toward the tangent. Nothing pushed it out.

W2.text: Aarav and his bike have a mass of sixty kilograms. He takes a flat ten metre turn at five metres per second, with mu zero point four. Will he skid?

W3.text: Friction needed, m v squared over r. Sixty times twenty five, over ten. One hundred and fifty newtons.

W4.text: Friction available, mu m g. Zero point four, times sixty, times nine point eight. About two hundred thirty five newtons.

W5.text: Needed is less than available, so he turns safely.

W6.text: His top speed is root mu r g. The root of thirty nine point two, about six point three metres per second.

X2.text: Many students draw two forces on the whirling stone. Tension, and a separate centripetal force.

X3.text: But there is only one force. The tension is the centripetal force.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In numericals on string tension, and top speed on a flat curve.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A disc turns at a steady five radians per second. For a coin on it, mu is zero point five, and g is ten. How far from the centre can the coin sit without slipping? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Twenty centimetres.

A2.text: Friction gives the centripetal force, so m omega squared r is at most mu m g.

A3.text: Cancel m. So r is at most mu g over omega squared.

A4.text: That is five, over twenty five. Zero point two metres, or twenty centimetres.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. What supplies the centripetal force for a stone on a string?

Y3.text: Two. Why does a car run wide on a flat curve if it goes too fast?

Y4.text: Three. Why does the top safe speed on a flat curve not depend on mass?

N1.text: Next time: how can a tilted road turn a car with no friction at all? We find out in banking of roads.
